parts.en: The clockwork: how mathematics describes the world
parts.pl: Mechanizm zegara: jak matematyka opisuje świat

chapters.label: ch:models
chapters.en: A model is a machine for predicting
chapters.brief: Argument: mathematics describes the world by building small machines that answer questions about it -- a state (a handful of numbers), a rule (how the numbers change), and a prediction (what the rule says the numbers will be later). A model is not a picture of reality; it is a question-answering device whose answers can be checked. The falling stone (distance after t seconds) and a cooling cup of tea are the two worked models; Halley's comet returning in 1758-59 and Laplace's demon (1814) are the high-water mark of the clockwork view, and Wigner's phrase from 1960 about the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics names it. The chapter ends by planting the book's question: if the rule is exact and known, is the future known? Payoff: the reader can name the state, the rule and the prediction of any model put in front of them, and can run a two-line Python model and read its output. Also introduces the laboratory: every number on the page is computed by a file under `code/`, and the reader is shown how to run one. Traps to elicit: a model is a copy of reality; a model that is wrong is useless; knowing the rule means knowing the future (planted, not yet refuted). Listings: the falling stone as a table; the cooling cup stepped minute by minute. One lab: write the stone's model and match a measured drop. Figures: a plot of the stone and the tea; a Mermaid diagram of state, rule, prediction.

chapters.label: ch:iteration
chapters.en: The rule of the next step
chapters.brief: Argument: the most important idea in the book is iteration -- a rule that turns today's state into tomorrow's, applied again and again: `x[n+1] = f(x[n])`. Savings at compound interest, a drug washing out of the blood, a cup cooling towards room temperature and a population with a fixed birth rate are all the same shape, `x[n+1] = a*x[n] + b`, and that shape has only three behaviours: grow without bound, shrink to nothing, or settle at a fixed point. Exponential growth and decay, doubling time and half-life, and the logarithm as the question how many steps until. Fixed points are where the rule leaves the state unchanged, and a fixed point is STABLE when a small nudge shrinks, which for this linear rule means the multiplier has size below one. The cobweb diagram is introduced here on a straight line, so that Chapter 5 can use it on a curve. Payoff: the reader can predict, without iterating, what a linear rule will do forever -- which is exactly the certainty the rest of the book takes away. Traps to elicit: exponential growth means fast growth (it means proportional growth, and it can be slow); a fixed point is where the system ends up (only if it is stable). Listings: iterating a rule; the doubling-time table; the cobweb data. One or two labs: find a fixed point and decide its stability; compute a doubling time with a logarithm. Figures: three linear rules and their three fates; a cobweb on a line.

chapters.label: ch:feedback
chapters.pl: Sprzężenie zwrotne: dlaczego nic nie rośnie wiecznie
chapters.brief: Argument: real growth slows because the thing that grows uses up what it grows on -- feedback -- and feedback makes a rule NONLINEAR: the effect of a change depends on where you already are. Verhulst's logistic growth (1838) and its S-curve, carrying capacity, and the difference between a straight-line rule and a curved one: for a linear rule two causes add (superposition), for a nonlinear one they do not. Local stability of a fixed point on a curve: zoom in until the curve looks straight, and the slope there -- measured numerically, as how much a tiny nudge is multiplied by one step -- decides whether nudges grow or die. This is the slope idea the rest of the book leans on, taught as a measurement rather than as calculus. The chapter ends on a discrete logistic population that settles smoothly for a gentle growth rate and then, turned up, overshoots and oscillates -- the hook for Chapter 5. Payoff: the reader can find the fixed points of a nonlinear rule, estimate the slope at each by computing, and predict which one the system approaches. Traps to elicit: the effect of two pushes is the sum of the effects (only for linear rules); a limit to growth means growth stops smoothly (it can overshoot and oscillate). Listings: continuous logistic growth stepped finely; numerical slope at a fixed point; the discrete logistic at two growth rates. Labs: estimate a slope numerically and classify a fixed point. Figures: exponential against logistic growth; the overshoot.

chapters.label: ch:motion
chapters.en: Motion: rules of change and the map of every state
chapters.pl: Ruch: reguły zmiany i mapa wszystkich stanów
chapters.brief: Argument: when time flows rather than ticks, the rule tells you the VELOCITY of the state rather than its next value -- a differential equation, read as a rule of change and never solved by hand here. Euler's method turns it back into iteration with a small step; the spring and the pendulum are the worked systems. The state of a pendulum is two numbers, angle and angular velocity, so its whole future is a curve through a plane of every possible state: the phase space, the one picture the rest of the book is drawn in. A frictionless pendulum draws closed loops (periodic, perfectly predictable); a damped one spirals into a fixed point (an attractor). Energy is the check: Euler's method visibly gains energy and spirals OUTWARD, a better method (Runge-Kutta, RK4, given as a recipe) holds it -- so the reader learns early that a simulation is not the system. Newton's two bodies trace ellipses forever: the clockwork at its best. Plant the theorem of Poincaré and Bendixson in one sentence: a smooth system with a two-number state cannot be chaotic, so chaos in a flow needs at least three numbers -- Chapter 9 cashes it. Payoff: the reader can turn a rule of change into a trajectory in code and read a phase portrait. Traps to elicit: a smaller step always makes a simulation right (it makes it right for longer); a pendulum is a simple system so its motion must be simple (true for one pendulum, false for two, Chapter 13). Listings: Euler and RK4 on a spring; the pendulum; energy drift. Labs: implement one RK4 step; measure energy drift. Figures: phase portrait of a pendulum; Euler spiralling out against RK4.

chapters.label: ch:logistic
chapters.en: One line of algebra, every kind of behaviour
chapters.pl: Jedna linijka algebry, każde możliwe zachowanie
chapters.brief: Argument: the discrete logistic rule `x[n+1] = r*x[n]*(1-x[n])` -- one multiplication short of the linear rules of Chapter 2 -- produces every behaviour the book is about as the single knob r is turned. r = 2.8 settles to a fixed point; r = 3.2 alternates between two values for ever; r = 3.5 cycles through four; r = 3.9 never repeats and never settles, although every value is produced by the same exact rule. The cobweb diagram from Chapter 2, now on a parabola, shows why: the fixed point's slope passes minus one and the fixed point loses its grip. Robert May's 1976 paper in Nature, written for ecologists, is the historical anchor, and its plea that everyone should meet this map early is the chapter's reason to exist. Payoff: the reader can iterate the map, draw its cobweb, find the fixed point `1 - 1/r` and say for which r it is stable -- and has seen irregular, never-repeating output come from a rule a child can compute. Traps to elicit: a simple rule gives simple behaviour; irregular output needs a random or complicated cause; if it has not repeated after a thousand steps it is about to. Listings: iterating the map at four values of r, in pure Python so every digit is reproducible; the cobweb data; period detection. Labs: detect the period of an orbit; find r where the fixed point loses stability. Figures: four time series; four cobwebs.

chapters.label: ch:butterfly
chapters.brief: Argument: sensitive dependence on initial conditions is not a metaphor but a measurement. Two runs of the logistic map at r = 4 that start one part in ten billion apart stay indistinguishable for a while, then separate completely within a few dozen steps -- counted exactly, in pure Python arithmetic, so the number of steps on the page is the same on every machine. The separation roughly doubles each step, so the error grows exponentially, which is Chapter 2's growth law now working against us. Edward Lorenz's 1961 discovery, when he restarted a run from a printout rounded to three decimals (0.506 for 0.506127) and got a different weather, and the title of his 1972 talk about a butterfly in Brazil. Determinism and predictability are two different properties: the map is perfectly deterministic -- the same start gives the same future, checked in code -- and still unpredictable in practice, because no start is known exactly. Payoff: the reader can measure how fast two nearby starts separate and say, for a given measurement error, how many steps a prediction is good for. Traps to elicit: chaos means random; the butterfly causes the tornado; if I rerun it I will get something different. Listings: two nearby runs side by side; the separation table; Lorenz's rounding reproduced on the logistic map. Labs: find the step at which two runs first differ by more than a tolerance. Figures: two trajectories peeling apart; separation on a log scale, a straight line then a ceiling.

chapters.label: ch:lyapunov
chapters.en: A number for chaos: the Lyapunov exponent
chapters.brief: Argument: the average rate at which nearby starts separate is a single number, the Lyapunov exponent -- the average of the logarithm of the stretching factor per step, `lambda = mean of log|f prime(x[n])|` -- positive for chaos, negative for a system that forgets its disturbances. For the logistic map at r = 4 it is exactly the natural logarithm of 2, which the reader computes and checks. Its reciprocal is the Lyapunov time, and the prediction horizon follows: steps until an error of size e0 reaches a tolerance T is about `log(T/e0)/lambda`. The payoff is the cruel arithmetic of that formula: measuring the start a thousand times more precisely buys only `log(1000)/lambda` more steps -- about ten at r = 4 -- so better instruments and bigger computers buy forecasts that are LONGER BY A CONSTANT, not proportionally longer. The exponent plotted against r shows chaos coming and going, with negative dips at the periodic windows. Payoff: the reader can compute a Lyapunov exponent from a time series of the map, turn it into a horizon, and explain why weather forecasts improve by days per decade rather than by weeks. Traps to elicit: ten times better data gives ten times longer forecasts; a bigger computer will eventually make any system predictable. Listings: the exponent by averaging; the horizon table against initial error; the exponent across r. Labs: compute the exponent for a given r; compute a prediction horizon. Figures: lambda against r; horizon against the logarithm of initial error, a straight line.

chapters.label: ch:bifurcations
chapters.en: The road to chaos, and a number nobody expected
chapters.pl: Droga do chaosu i liczba, której nikt się nie spodziewał
chapters.brief: Argument: the whole of Chapter 5 fits in one picture -- the bifurcation diagram, the long-run values of x plotted against r -- and the picture has structure. Period one splits to two, two to four, four to eight, at parameter values that crowd together geometrically; the ratio of successive gaps tends to Feigenbaum's constant, about 4.669, which the reader computes from the map's superstable parameters. The same number comes out of a completely different rule (the sine map `x[n+1] = s*sin(pi*x[n])`), which is universality: the number belongs to the route, not to the equation -- and it has been measured in real fluids and circuits, within the precision of those experiments. Inside the chaos there are windows of order; the period-3 window opens at `r = 1 + sqrt(8)`, and Li and Yorke's 1975 paper title, period three implies chaos, says what that means. Payoff: the reader can draw a bifurcation diagram, compute the first few period-doubling parameters and Feigenbaum's ratio, and explain why a constant of nature can come out of a toy model. Traps to elicit: the transition from order to chaos is a sudden switch; a different equation gives a different route; chaos, once reached, is everywhere beyond it. Listings: the bifurcation data; superstable parameters by bisection; the ratios for two maps. Labs: locate a superstable parameter; compute a Feigenbaum ratio. Figures: the bifurcation diagram; a zoom showing self-similarity; the ratios converging.

chapters.label: ch:lorenz
chapters.en: Three equations for the weather: the Lorenz attractor
chapters.pl: Trzy równania na pogodę: atraktor Lorenza
chapters.brief: Argument: chaos is not a quirk of stepping rules; it lives in continuous time too, and Lorenz found it in 1963 in three equations cut down from a model of convection (sigma = 10, rho = 28, beta = 8/3), in his paper Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow. Integrated with Chapter 4's RK4, the state wanders round two lobes, switching unpredictably between them, and never repeats -- three numbers is exactly what Chapter 4's theorem said chaos in a flow needs. Two starts a hair apart diverge, and the rate is a Lyapunov exponent of about 0.9 per time unit, measured here. And yet the trajectory never leaves a bounded butterfly-shaped set: the attractor. That is the chapter's hinge and the book's second big idea: the INDIVIDUAL future is unpredictable, but WHERE the system lives and HOW OFTEN it visits each region is perfectly predictable. Statistics of the attractor -- the fraction of time on each lobe, the average height -- are stable numbers, the same from almost any start. Payoff: the reader can integrate the Lorenz system, measure its divergence, and compute a statistic of the attractor that does not depend on the start. Traps to elicit: a chaotic system can go anywhere; if the path is unpredictable nothing about it is predictable; chaos needs many variables. Listings: RK4 on the Lorenz system; divergence of two runs; lobe statistics from different starts. Labs: implement the Lorenz derivative; measure a lobe fraction. Figures: the attractor in projection; two runs diverging; a histogram that does not care about the start.

chapters.label: ch:strange
chapters.brief: Argument: every chaotic system does two things over and over -- it STRETCHES (nearby points separate, the positive Lyapunov exponent) and FOLDS (the stretched set is put back into a bounded region, or it would fly apart). A baker kneading dough is the picture, Smale's horseshoe is the mathematics in words, and the Henon map (1976, a = 1.4, b = 0.3) is a two-line rule that does it. Each step of the Henon map shrinks area by the factor |b|, computed as a determinant and checked by measuring, so the attractor has zero area -- and yet stretching gives it infinite length. Zooming in repeatedly on the attractor shows the same layered structure at every scale, which is what makes it strange rather than merely odd, and hands the geometry to Chapter 11. Payoff: the reader can iterate the Henon map, show that a cloud of starting points collapses onto the same attractor, measure the area contraction and the Lyapunov exponent, and explain chaos as stretch plus fold. Traps to elicit: shrinking area means the motion dies out; a bounded system cannot be sensitive to its start; zooming in on a curve always ends with a straight line. Listings: the Henon map; a cloud of starts collapsing; area contraction measured. Labs: implement one Henon step and its area factor. Figures: the attractor; two successive zooms; a square stretched and folded after a few steps.

chapters.label: ch:fractals
chapters.en: Fractals: measuring what has no length
chapters.pl: Fraktale: mierzenie czegoś, co nie ma długości
chapters.brief: Argument: the shapes chaos leaves behind are fractals, and fractals break the idea of length. The Cantor set (1883) and Koch's snowflake curve (1904) are built by iteration; the Koch curve's length multiplies by 4/3 at every stage, so it has no finite length while enclosing a finite area. Lewis Fry Richardson's measurements of coastlines and borders and Mandelbrot's 1967 paper in Science asking how long the coast of Britain is: the measured length grows as the ruler shrinks, along a straight line on a log-log plot whose slope gives a dimension between one and two. Dimension becomes a measurement -- box counting -- and the reader computes it for the Koch curve (log 4 / log 3, about 1.26) and for Chapter 10's Henon attractor (also about 1.26, by coincidence, which the chapter says). Nature's fractals, stated carefully: coastlines, river networks, lungs and blood vessels are fractal over a range of scales, not all the way down. Payoff: the reader can compute a box-counting dimension, read a log-log plot, and say what a non-integer dimension claims. Traps to elicit: a coastline has a length; dimension must be a whole number; fractals are decoration. Listings: building the Koch curve and counting its length; box counting on the Koch curve and on the Henon attractor. Labs: implement box counting; compute the Cantor set's dimension. Figures: Koch stages; the log-log plot of boxes against box size.

chapters.label: ch:mandelbrot
chapters.en: Iterating in the plane: Julia and Mandelbrot
chapters.pl: Iteracja na płaszczyźnie: Julia i Mandelbrot
chapters.brief: Argument: iterate the simplest nonlinear rule, `z[n+1] = z[n]*z[n] + c`, on points of a plane instead of a line, and the question will this escape to infinity draws the most famous shapes in mathematics. Complex numbers are introduced from zero as points of the plane with a rule for multiplying them (lengths multiply, angles add) and Python's built-in complex type does the arithmetic. For a fixed c, the points that do not escape form a Julia set (Julia and Fatou, around 1918); the set of c for which the orbit of zero does not escape is the Mandelbrot set, drawn by computer from about 1980. The escape radius 2 is proved in one line. The payoff connects the book: the logistic map is the same rule in disguise (a change of variables turns `r*x*(1-x)` into `z*z + c` with `c = r/2 - r*r/4`), so the real axis of the Mandelbrot set IS Chapter 8's bifurcation diagram -- the period-doubling points and the period-3 window sit exactly where the conversion says, checked numerically. Payoff: the reader can compute escape times, draw a Julia set and the Mandelbrot set at low resolution, and convert between r and c. Traps to elicit: complex numbers are imaginary so they describe nothing real; the Mandelbrot set is a picture of chaos (its boundary is where chaos lives); infinite detail means infinite information. Listings: complex multiplication by hand and by Python; escape time; the r-to-c conversion checked against Chapter 8's numbers. Labs: implement escape time; convert Feigenbaum points to c. Figures: the Mandelbrot set; two Julia sets, one connected and one dust; the real axis against the bifurcation diagram.

chapters.label: ch:mechanics
chapters.brief: Argument: the clockwork of Chapter 1 was built on mechanics, and mechanics is where chaos was first seen. Hang a second pendulum from the first and the motion becomes chaotic: two double pendulums released a fraction of a degree apart swing together, then apart, measured here with energy conservation as the check that the divergence is physics and not numerical error. Poincaré found the same in the three-body problem while competing for King Oscar II's prize (the memoir published in 1890), and his corrected work is the first description of chaos. The solar system itself is chaotic on long timescales: Laskar's 1989 computation gives a Lyapunov time of about five million years for the inner planets, which means the positions of the planets cannot be predicted a hundred million years ahead even though their orbits will stay roughly where they are for billions -- the attractor idea again, as bounded unpredictability. Friction-free mechanics conserves energy and so has no attractor; chaos there is a sea around islands of regular motion, stated in words (KAM) and shown with a double pendulum at low and high energy. Payoff: the reader can simulate a double pendulum, check energy conservation, measure divergence, and separate the parts of the solar-system story that are measured from those that are folklore. Traps to elicit: the solar system is a perfect clock; a system that conserves energy cannot be chaotic; chaos needs friction or randomness. Listings: the double pendulum with RK4 and an energy check; divergence of two releases; low against high energy. Labs: implement the energy function; find the time two releases separate. Figures: two double pendulum tips diverging; energy error against time.

chapters.label: ch:weather
chapters.en: Weather, climate and the ensemble forecast
chapters.brief: Argument: weather forecasting is the place chaos theory changed practice most. Because the atmosphere has a positive Lyapunov exponent and many scales of motion, Lorenz argued in 1969 that detailed weather has a finite predictability of about two weeks however good the data -- the commonly quoted figure, labelled as such. Forecasters answered with the ENSEMBLE: run the model many times from slightly different starts consistent with what was measured, and report the spread -- a forecast becomes a probability. The reader builds one on the Lorenz system and on Lorenz's 1996 forty-variable toy atmosphere: the ensemble spread grows with lead time, and the spread itself says how far ahead the forecast is worth trusting. Weather against climate: climate is the statistics of the attractor, which Chapter 9 showed are predictable when individual paths are not, so the claim that we cannot predict the weather next month so we cannot predict climate confuses the path with the attractor -- and changing a parameter (the forcing) moves the statistics, which is what a climate projection asks. Payoff: the reader can build an ensemble forecast, read its spread as confidence, compute a probability from it, and separate a weather question from a climate question. Traps to elicit: a forecast is a single number; if the weather is unpredictable the climate is too; a 30 per cent chance of rain forecast that was followed by rain was wrong. Listings: an ensemble on the Lorenz system; ensemble spread against lead time; Lorenz-96 ensemble; climate statistics under two parameter values. Labs: turn an ensemble into a probability; measure the lead time at which spread saturates. Figures: an ensemble plume fanning out; spread against lead time; statistics shifting with a parameter.

chapters.label: ch:life
chapters.en: Life, markets and noise: telling chaos from chance
chapters.pl: Życie, rynki i szum: jak odróżnić chaos od przypadku
chapters.brief: Argument: chaos is claimed for populations, epidemics, hearts, brains and markets, and the reader should be able to judge the claims. Populations: May's map was written for ecology, and Costantino and colleagues' 1997 flour-beetle experiment in Science pushed a real population through period doubling into chaos by manipulating adult mortality. Epidemics: the basic SIR model settles, but seasonal forcing (children returning to school) can make it chaotic, which is one reading of pre-vaccine measles records. Hearts and brains: rhythms, arrhythmias, and why healthy variability is not the same as chaos (stated as contested). Markets: prices are irregular, and irregular is not evidence of chaos. The core skill is TELLING CHAOS FROM NOISE: a chaotic series and a random series can have the same histogram, yet plotting each value against the next (a return map) shows a curve for the chaotic series and a cloud for the random one, and a chaotic series is predictable a step or two ahead by looking up its nearest past neighbours while noise is not. The reader applies both tests and then applies them to noisy chaos, where they get harder -- short noisy data can make anything look like anything. Payoff: the reader can generate chaotic and random series with the same distribution, tell them apart with a return map and a nearest-neighbour forecast, and say what evidence a claim of chaos in real data needs. Traps to elicit: irregular data proves chaos; chaos in markets means you can predict them; a random-looking sequence must come from randomness. Listings: logistic series against shuffled series; return maps; nearest-neighbour forecast error against horizon; a seasonally forced SIR model. Labs: build a return map test; build a nearest-neighbour predictor. Figures: two histograms that match and two return maps that do not; forecast error against horizon for chaos and noise.

chapters.label: ch:computers
chapters.brief: Argument: a computer simulating a chaotic system is itself a slightly different system, because every step rounds. Floating-point numbers are introduced from zero (a fixed number of significant binary digits), and the logistic map run in single and in double precision parts company after a predictable number of steps -- the prediction horizon of Chapter 7 with the rounding error as the initial error. The doubling map `x -> 2x mod 1` run on doubles collapses to exactly zero after about fifty-odd steps, because each step shifts out one binary digit and the machine has only fifty-three -- a chaotic map that the computer cannot even represent. And yet simulations are not worthless: the shadowing idea says that for many chaotic systems a computed orbit stays close to SOME true orbit from a slightly different start, so statistics come out right even when the path is wrong -- which is why Chapter 9's lobe fractions survive. Reproducibility: the same code on two machines can diverge when a single operation rounds differently, which is why this book's own numbers use only correctly rounded arithmetic and are checked in CI. Where this meets AI: training a network multiplies many Jacobians, and the growth rate of that product is a Lyapunov exponent -- exploding and vanishing gradients are chaos and its opposite; random recurrent networks have a transition to chaos (Sompolinsky, Crisanti and Sommers, 1988); pseudo-random numbers are deliberately chaotic arithmetic. Payoff: the reader can predict when a float32 simulation will part from a float64 one, explain the doubling-map collapse, and say which results of a chaotic simulation can be trusted. Traps to elicit: a deterministic program always gives the same answer; more decimal places make a simulation exact; a chaotic map makes a good random-number generator. Listings: float32 against float64 logistic; the doubling map collapse; shadowing illustrated by statistics that agree; a product of random matrices growing. Labs: count steps until float32 and float64 disagree; predict the doubling-map collapse step. Figures: two precisions parting company; the product of Jacobians growing or shrinking.

chapters.label: ch:taming
chapters.brief: Argument: sensitivity cuts both ways. If a tiny disturbance changes the future a lot, then a tiny, well-timed push can steer it a lot -- which is the idea of Ott, Grebogi and Yorke's 1990 paper Controlling Chaos. A chaotic attractor is full of unstable periodic orbits; wait until the state passes near one and nudge the parameter slightly, and the system can be held on an orbit it would never keep by itself. The reader stabilises the logistic map's unstable fixed point at r = 3.9 with parameter nudges of under one per cent, and measures how small the nudges are. Synchronisation: two identical chaotic systems, one driving the other through a single variable, lock together (Pecora and Carroll, 1990), shown on the Lorenz system -- the idea behind proposals to hide a message in chaotic noise. The chapter keeps claims in proportion: control of chaos has been demonstrated in lasers, circuits and heart tissue in the laboratory; it is not a routine clinical or industrial technique, and the chapter says so. Payoff: the reader can implement a small-nudge controller, show it stabilising an unstable orbit, and synchronise two Lorenz systems through one coupling. Traps to elicit: chaos cannot be controlled; controlling a system means overpowering it; two chaotic systems can never agree. Listings: the uncontrolled and controlled logistic map; nudge sizes; drive-response Lorenz synchronisation error. Labs: implement the controller rule; measure synchronisation time. Figures: control switched on mid-run; synchronisation error falling to zero.

chapters.label: ch:why
chapters.en: Why you need chaos: a field guide to prediction
chapters.pl: Po co ci chaos: przewodnik terenowy po przewidywaniu
chapters.brief: Argument: the book's conclusion, stated as a practical skill rather than a sentiment. Knowing chaos theory changes what you do: you ask for the horizon of any prediction, you prefer an ensemble to a point, you separate questions about paths from questions about statistics, you stop attributing big effects to small causes after the fact, you distrust patterns in short irregular data, and you check that a simulation's answer survives a change of step size and precision. The chapter collects the book's measurements into one table of horizons (logistic map, Lorenz, Henon, double pendulum, the solar system as quoted) and turns them into seven questions to ask of any forecast, model or claim -- each question citing the chapter where the reader measured it. It also says plainly what chaos theory is NOT: not a theory of everything, not complexity or disorder in general, not an excuse for fatalism (the climate and the control chapters say why), and not a licence to call anything unpredictable butterfly-shaped. The reader leaves able to explain to a colleague, with numbers they computed, why some things can be predicted for a century and others not for a fortnight. Payoff: the field guide. Traps to elicit (the last catalogue check): unpredictable means unknowable; chaos means anything goes; small causes always matter. Listings: the horizon table recomputed from the book's own values. Labs: apply the seven questions to a model the reader writes. Figures: the map of predictability -- horizon against error for every system in the book on one plot.
